# Introduction {#sec-intro}

In many classification problems the class we care about is rare. Fraudulent
card payments, a rare disease picked up in screening, or a machine part that
is about to fail can each make up 1% of cases or far fewer. In the credit card
data we use later, only 492 of 284,807 transactions (0.17%) are fraud. A
"classifier" that calls every transaction normal is therefore 99.83% accurate,
and it never catches a single fraud. Fraud teams face exactly this problem in
practice, where the rare class is also the expensive one
[@carcillo2021; @leborgne2022].

This is the class imbalance problem. Overall accuracy rewards a model for
ignoring the rare class, and a model fitted by maximum likelihood and used
with the usual 0.5 cutoff flags very few cases as positive. Three kinds of
remedy are commonly recommended [@he2009]. The first is resampling: change
the training data so the two classes are the same size, either by copying
rare-class rows (over-sampling), dropping common-class rows (under-sampling),
or creating synthetic rare-class rows with SMOTE [@chawla2002]. The second is
to give each rare-class row a larger weight in the fit. The third is to keep
the model as it is and lower the cutoff above which a case is called
positive.

All three make the model flag more positives, so sensitivity goes up. That is
not the same thing as a better model. A model predicts well when it ranks
positives above negatives and when its probabilities can be trusted.
Sensitivity at a single cutoff mixes the quality of the model with the choice
of cutoff, so a remedy can raise it without the model having learned anything
new. Recent work in medical risk prediction has raised exactly this concern,
finding that imbalance corrections can make logistic models worse calibrated
without making them better at telling the classes apart
[@vandengoorbergh2022; @carriero2025]. Whether SMOTE in particular helps
strong classifiers has also been questioned [@elor2022]. Our research
question is therefore:

> **When positives are rare, do the standard remedies improve prediction, or
> do they only improve the metric?**

We study it in two ways. The first is a simulation study in which we write
down the true model ourselves, so we know the best performance any method
could reach and can tell a real improvement from a shifted cutoff. The second
is the Kaggle credit card fraud data [@dalpozzolo2015], where the truth is
unknown but the problem is a real one. We use two classifiers from opposite
ends of the flexibility scale covered in the course: lasso logistic
regression [@islr2, Section 6.2.2] and random forests [@islr2, Section 8.2.2].
For the STAT 847 part of the project we also build EasyEnsemble [@liu2009],
which combines several under-sampled models, and ask whether combining weak
learners does better than any single remedy. Finally, one of us wrote a
second, independent version of the whole study with different software,
which we use as a robustness check.

All three team members contributed equally to this project. The code, saved
results and the source of this report are on GitHub at
<https://github.com/Anyanso/stat447-team2-imbalance>.
